questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests systemd mastery: timers, dependencies, failure handling, and idempotent logging.

## Key Concepts
- systemd timer and service wiring
- network-online.target dependency
- OnFailure retry flow
- centralized log rotation for backup logs

## Code Example
```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/backup.service
[Unit]
Description=Nightly backup
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/daily-backup.sh
StandardOutput=append:/var/log/backup.log
StandardError=append:/var/log/backup.log
```
```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer
[Unit]
Description=Daily backup timer

[Timer]
OnCalendar=daily 02:00
Persistent=true
Unit=backup.service

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```
```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/backup.service.d/override.conf
[Unit]
OnFailure=backup-retry.service
```
```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/backup-retry.service
[Unit]
Description=Retry backup after failure
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/bin/bash -lc 'sleep 900; /usr/local/bin/daily-backup.sh'
```
```ini
# /etc/logrotate.d/backup
/var/log/backup.log {
  daily
  rotate 7
  compress
  missingok
  notifempty
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you add a health check to prevent overlap with a running backup?
- How would you audit and alert on failures?

questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
- Tests practical log management and prevention of log loss in a real service
- Checks understanding of rotation cadence, backup retention, and service interaction

Key Concepts
- logrotate stanza syntax and options (weekly, rotate, compress, missingok, notifempty, copytruncate, sharedscripts)
- Post-rotation actions to refresh services (nginx log file handles)
- Impact of log rotation on running daemons and data integrity

Code Example
```bash
/var/log/myapp/*.log {
    weekly
    rotate 4
    compress
    missingok
    notifempty
    copytruncate
    sharedscripts
    postrotate
        systemctl reload nginx >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    endscript
}
```

How This Prevents Log Loss
- `copytruncate` copies the current log to a new file, then truncates the original, ensuring continuous logging without interruption
- `sharedscripts` ensures the postrotate command runs only once per rotation, preventing multiple nginx reloads
- `missingok` and `notifempty` prevent errors if logs don't exist or are empty, avoiding rotation failures
- `systemctl reload nginx` gracefully reopens log file handles without dropping connections, preventing log loss during rotation

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates practical skills in provisioning a containerized backup pipeline with real-world constraints, including idempotent operations, zero-downtime reloads, and hardened security boundaries.

## Key Concepts
- Podman container lifecycle for backup operations
- rsync over SSH with snapshot retention policies
- systemd timers and drop-ins for zero-downtime service reloads
- SELinux policy minimalism for containerized tasks
- nftables rules for outbound SSH and stateful inbound replies
- Integrity validation using sha256 checksums and rollback procedures

## Code Example
```bash
# Container run with SSH keys mounted
podman run --name backup-agent \\
  -v /data:/data:ro \\
  -v ~/.ssh/backup_keys:/root/.ssh:ro \\
  -v /backup snapshots:/backup-snapshots \\
  docker.io/library/backup-agent:latest \
  /usr/local/bin/backup.sh

# systemd timer for hourly runs
cat > /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer <<EOF
[Unit]
Description=Hourly Backup Timer

[Timer]
OnCalendar=hourly
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
EOF

# systemd drop-in for zero-downtime reloads
mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/backup.service.d
cat > /etc/systemd/system/backup.service.d/10-zero-downtime.conf <<EOF
[Service]
ExecReload=
ExecReload=podman kill --signal=SIGHUP backup-agent
EOF

# Minimal SELinux policy for container backup
cat > backup.te <<EOF
module backup 1.0;

require {
    type container_t;
    type ssh_home_t;
    class dir { read getattr };
    class file { read getattr };
}

allow container_t ssh_home_t:dir { read getattr };
allow container_t ssh_home_t:file { read getattr };
EOF

# nftables rules for SSH
nft add rule ip filter OUTPUT tcp dport 22 accept
nft add rule ip filter INPUT ct state established,related accept
```

```bash
sudo chown sftpu:sftpu /srv/sftp/sftpu/uploads

# 2) Configure SSHD
sudo tee -a /etc/ssh/sshd_config << 'EOF'

Match User sftpu
    ChrootDirectory /srv/sftp
    ForceCommand internal-sftp
    X11Forwarding no
    AllowTcpForwarding no
EOF

sudo systemctl restart sshd
sudo passwd sftpu
sftp sftpu@localhost
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests end-to-end familiarity with containerized TLS termination, dynamic config, and production hardening: watcher-driven reloads, firewall hardening, and zero-downtime upgrades.

## Key Concepts
- Podman-based TLS termination
- Inotify watcher and USR2/zero-downtime reloads
- nftables with a dynamically loaded set for outbound control
- systemd drop-ins for rolling upgrades
- minimal SELinux policy for container permissions

## Code Example
```bash
# Example: systemd drop-in for zero-downtime reload
# /etc/systemd/system/nginx-tls.service.d/reload.conf
[Service]
ExecReload=/usr/sbin/nginx -s reload -c /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test rollback after a failed reload?
- How would you audit and rotate the backends.json securely?
